If “intellect in act” means an actual intelligible form, as in Farabi’s account, then there is no problem: the human soul always has at least one basic intelligible idea. But the objection means intellect in act in the stronger sense of the Active Intellect, or at least the third stage of the soul’s intellect. Avicenna’s account of separation includes freedom from time, place, direction, and potentiality, so the problem remains if the soul is separate from its first moment.
Bodily makeup may give the soul a good power of reasoning, quick insight, or sacred insight. The soul’s actions may also grow stronger through practice and good habits.

One reply is that being separate by nature does not make the soul an actual intellect from the start. In Avicenna’s view, the soul’s knowledge of particular things is a later perfection. It depends on earlier sense and imagination, which prepare the soul to form universal intellectual ideas. So the soul’s existence as a separate substance does not mean that all its intellectual powers are already actual.

Two arguments for the soul's freedom from matter have been indicated here. First, the soul must be free from matter because what it understands is free from matter. Second, it can grasp true unity and simplicity. But these arguments prove the point only for souls that have actually reached those abilities, and such souls are very few. For the author, to understand horse in a purely intellectual way is to become one with the intellect that governs that kind—or at least to grasp the horse as something understood in act. That is not simply the bare meaning of "horse": a nature without existence is nothing. It is one real existence that gathers many things together, even if a thousand intellects grasp it. It is the same reality present in the fully actual intellects. Each such object of understanding exists as a luminous reality free from matter, place, direction, position and time, yet includes everything belonging to its own kind. None of its intelligible features or its outward instances falls outside its knowledge. Its hearing and sight are its immediate knowledge of what is heard and seen; its hands and feet, or power of movement, are its effective knowledge and power. The senses and limbs of the natural beings belonging to that kind are lower expressions of what is present in it. The existence of an intellect is simple but embraces its many manifestations, and even their further manifestations. In that sense it is both what gives knowledge and what is known; through knowing it, we may learn about them. As for the second argument, how many people really understand a unity and simplicity in which nothing is put together out of what it has and what it lacks? Only a few who have reached the highest degrees of understanding.

It is surprising to call the acquired intellect and the Active Intellect the same kind when one is dependent and the other is what it depends on, and when one has passed through matter while the other has never been in matter. Some philosophers do not accept that members of one kind can differ in this way.

The comparison with sunlight applies to the relation between outside colors and their visible forms: colors are only visible in potentiality in the dark and become visible in light. What is directly visible is the form present to sight, not the outside color as it exists in matter. In the same way, an intelligible form receives existence from its separate source. The direct object of sight or knowledge may be called the visible or intelligible thing itself, because its image is present to the perceiver. The form is what we look through; it is not a second image inside another image. Just as light is visible by itself and makes colors visible, intellectual light is present by itself and makes intelligible forms visible. The mind should see the Active Intellect in the forms it understands, since the intellect’s existence is the shared existence of those forms.
This is the view held by Aristotle’s followers. The Illuminationists instead speak of a guiding form for each kind of thing.
This assumes that images of things exist in the Active Intellect in a cause-and-effect order.

It is strange that these forms are ordered but do not exist there as separate forms or as forms lodged in a subject. One explanation is that they are not separate from the Active Intellect: they are connected aspects of its one existence, which remain with it. The intellect contains the existence of things in a higher, simpler way; their essences follow from that existence. Their order is therefore a matter of how we understand the forms.

The point of the claim that self-awareness lasts is to distinguish this argument from the previous one and to establish the basic reality of direct awareness: the self is immediately present to itself.

This is the same kind of case: if an immaterial self knew itself through a mental image, the image and self would differ in how they exist, just as an idea in the mind differs from an outside individual. That difference is compatible with the image matching the self in nature.
In other words, self-knowledge through direct awareness can coexist with conceptual knowledge of oneself. We can also form ideas about our own thinking.

The earlier proof says that a mental image differs from the outside thing. This proof says that a universal image differs from the particular individual. It may be one argument expressed in two ways: what we know, and our knowledge of it, are both particular, so neither is simply a universal image.
“Not in a subject” is only part of the definition of a substance. A substance is a nature that exists in itself, rather than as a feature of something else.
The self’s not being hidden from itself is direct, existential awareness. That is why the speaker says that nothing remains but existence.
This is conceptual awareness, added to direct awareness. It does not make the self what it is, nor does it make awareness of anything else identical with the self’s existence.

The actual referent of “I” is the existence of the one who perceives himself. Since that existence is immaterial, it is not hidden from itself. The word “I” can be used of the Necessary Being and of other beings, but here it means any real being that is aware of itself.

If the objection is that the soul is existence and the Necessary Being is existence, so the soul must be the Necessary Being, the argument confuses a general concept with real existence. If it is framed as a formal syllogism, it is invalid. Or, if the claim is that anything whose nonexistence is impossible must be the Necessary Being, Sadra replies that the soul’s existence is limited and incomplete, while the Necessary Being is existence in its fullest perfection.
Any act of will or desire also includes awareness and love of oneself.
In every case listed, knowledge of the object includes awareness of oneself.

We cannot know a cause by way of its effect, or one effect by way of another, if doing so requires moving from the effect back to its cause and then to another effect. If we could infer our self from our own action, this would be possible. The two kinds of indirect proof under discussion do not establish knowledge in such cases. In general necessary connections that do not involve causation, indirect proof can still provide knowledge.
The argument is first stated in reverse: a material thing cannot understand an intelligible form. From this it follows that anything that does understand such a form is free of matter.

The natural universal can be said of particular individuals. When we call something by a general name, what matters is the meaning of that name. The natural universal is the nature of a thing considered just as it is, and the meaning applies to the individuals in which that nature exists.

But the intellectual universal, considered as a separate object of thought, cannot be said of individuals in the same way. On the account used here, it has an immaterial existence of its own and is even the governing reality of the kind.

You may ask: do we not often say that the intellectual universal gathers the existence of its individuals in a fuller way, and that it is those individuals? Yes, but that is not ordinary predication. Separate realities are not said of one another in that way. Rather, an image is in one respect the thing it images, while the original possesses what is shown in the image in a higher way. The natural universal can also be said of the intellectual universal.

The natural kind, taken simply as what it is, is not called divisible or indivisible at the level of the concept. In actual individuals it is divided. So it is not a case of something actually indivisible being one with something actually divided.
This is not a legal analogy or a formal logical example. It is only meant to suggest that something spatial could be one with something nonspatial.
There is a difference between being nonspatial without being defined by that feature, as with prime matter, and being nonspatial by nature, as with an intellectual universal.
The separate parts would have to stand apart from the whole as a condition does from what depends on it.
The second contradiction is that if the parts differed in shape or number, the whole would not be intelligible as one kind.

The object of understanding is supposed to be indivisible. If its intelligibility depends on two parts, it must be divided. The wording also allows another reading: the parts are only introduced as conditions in the argument, while the thing itself is assumed to be simple.

The first option assumes that the intellect is located at the endpoint of the thing it understands; the second assumes that the intellect and what it understands become one. In either case, the endpoint would be the boundary of the intellect’s own measurable extent.

The image is not really taken from something outside. The enormous circle could be in the sky, but the surrounding square is not an outside shape. The alternative—that it exists in brain matter—is also rejected.
The first difficulty concerns size; the second concerns shape. Shape is a way of being arranged within a size.

The point is not simply that a potential perceiver cannot cause an actual image. Rather, if the image were the form received by the faculty, it would be a material subject and the faculty would be a substance, reversing the required relationship. If the imagined shape were the agent and the faculty were affected by it, then an image, which is only a feature, would be stronger than the faculty, which is a substance.
An extended quantity cannot be directly present to itself in every part; its parts are distinct from each other and from the whole. But an efficient cause must be more fully present to its effect.

Bodily powers act gradually and need a spatial relation to the matter their effects arise from. Imagined forms arise all at once, with no matter to establish such a relation beforehand. Their making is more like creation by a simple command than a bodily action carried out over time.
“As the one perceiving” preserves the difference between the soul’s powers. The soul is one, but it understands universal ideas and perceives images through different levels or powers.

The author is right: this proof establishes that imagination—or the soul at the level of imagination—is free of ordinary matter. Here the "place" of imagined forms means what produces them, not a container that passively receives them. Still, the philosophers' claim can be defended in a limited sense: the proof establishes that the soul is nonmaterial in some respect, and that may be enough as a first step. Further arguments must distinguish its freedom from matter from freedom from dimensions and, beyond that, from dependence on any distinct nature or essence. That is how their interpretation can be understood.
If the soul does not take on the square’s shape, there is no specific relation by which that square exists in it.
The discussion of cause and effect can be shortened: imagined forms are present to the soul as its effects, much as bodily forms are present to the soul without making it take on their shapes.

The imagined form may come from a separate imaginal source, just as intellectual forms come from the Active Intellect. Once the soul has acquired and retained a form, it may also be attributed to the soul as its producer. The form is present to the soul as a perfection is present to something less complete, not by being lodged in it as matter.

The mirror example works whether reflected images are understood as forms in an imaginal world, as some Illuminationists say, or as reflections of natural things, as Sadra says. On Sadra’s view, the soul produces even mirror images by arranging mirrors.
This follows the theory that vision works through rays emitted from the eye.

The author gives two answers: prime matter is not actually free of size in reality, and its lack of a fixed size is not the same as the intellect’s being inherently nonspatial. The brain, by contrast, is bound to bodily extension.
The soul is not defined by being bodily, while the brain is defined by its small, measurable size.

The argument concerns blackness and whiteness being present together in the same act of judgment, not merely one after the other. “Imagination” here may refer to the shared inner sense that judges them, not only the faculty that stores images.
On the usual view, the forms exist in the mind by being received in it. On Sadra’s view, they exist by the mind’s productive act. Either way, the forms of both opposites must be present.
This is offered as a possible reply to the objection; Sadra’s stronger answer follows.
The word “or” here means “and”: the argument needs both points. Bodily things cannot produce imagined forms, because material action requires a spatial relation.

Since the questioner claims that the soul receives images as features, the reply accepts that assumption for the sake of the argument: a feature essential to the image cannot fail to be present in the image.
If forms exist in the mind through the mind’s own productive act, there is no need to treat them as features that make the mind hot, cold, black, or white.

The opposites can belong to one body at the same time, but only in different parts; they cannot be present together in one undivided subject. The argument can be set out this way: the soul or imagination cannot simultaneously know and fail to know the very same thing—for example, what is written in Zayd's book. An extended body, however, can admit opposites in distinct parts. If the soul or imagination were bodily, such a division would be possible in it; but the consequence is false. So the soul's power to imagine cannot be bodily in that way.
A point cannot itself be the subject that receives a feature. Its actual subject would be the measurable thing whose boundary it is, and that would be extended.

Earlier philosophers treated the inner powers as states of the body or its subtle life-spirit, so they would disappear when the body falls apart. On the author’s view, these inner powers are nonbodily and remain with the soul when it leaves the body, preserving its way of perceiving particulars.
Here “essential” and “necessary” have the same sense.

Even if the soul has no intellectual life before birth, it can reach this state after birth. The nature becomes actual through an individual, so the soul may acquire intellect as it develops. On this account, the soul is a lower, less complete level of intellect, while the simple intellect is its fuller inner reality.

The soul's "first source" may mean the First Cause—God—or its nearer source, the Active Intellect. Either way, describing the soul as ancient is not merely using the name of its cause for the soul, or applying a description of one thing to something connected with it. All light is one reality: its levels differ in priority, completeness and strength, from the most dazzling light to governing and guiding lights, not in the basic reality of light. In that sense the eternity of the source may be spoken of as the soul's eternity. This gives Plato's words a plausible interpretation, but it does not establish that his view is correct. The soul, properly speaking, is the stage of life connected with the body, and that stage begins in time. It begins with bodily existence and changes in its very being until it can endure as spiritual life.
The argument uses a conditional construction: if knowledge were not essential, then the soul’s lack of knowledge would be. Sadra challenges that move in the next paragraph.

The argument can also be framed by saying that a soul with no capacity for understanding would never understand. But it still overlooks the difference between lacking knowledge essentially and being able to gain it. Its answer is the one Sadra gives in the main text.

The first mistake is to assume that because the soul lacks knowledge, this lack must be essential. The second is to confuse absolute lack of knowledge with not having a particular kind of knowledge at a particular stage.
The sharper wording is that the possible thing would be impossible forever, not merely absent forever.

The claim is that being absorbed in bodily life blocks awareness of knowledge already present in the soul. Sadra replies that if an intelligible form is actually present to an immaterial soul, that very presence is awareness. Otherwise, every uneducated person would already have all knowledge in a hidden, simple form.
An uneducated soul has not yet developed the ability to recover universal ideas from such a storehouse, because it has not first understood them.

If mere potential connection to forms in the Active Intellect counted as knowing them, every soul would already know them all. This would make the claim that the soul knew them before embodiment a symbolic account, not literal knowledge.

A concept sought through thought may be unknown in its essence but known by a description or feature. Or it may be unknown in one feature and known through another. The known parts allow the search to begin, while the thing sought remains unknown in the relevant respect.

Perhaps the difficulty is this: what is already known cannot be acquired, because that would be acquiring something we already have; what is unknown cannot be acquired either, since we cannot seek what we do not know. The answer is that these are not two things, but one thing known in one respect and unknown in another. Its known and unknown aspects belong to one existence. It is like claiming that nothing can be complete in one respect and incomplete in another, because the complete aspect is wholly complete and the incomplete aspect wholly incomplete. That claim is plainly false. The objection about learning fails for the same reason.

The previous argument also dealt with this topic, but there the point was to show that the knower is immaterial; the immateriality of what is known was only part of the route to that conclusion. Here, the immateriality of what is known is itself the point.
That is, no power belonging to a body can perceive it. Here “power” first means a receptive power, and “a power in a body” means an active power.
Whether perception is passive, as most philosophers think, or active, as the author holds, it still requires a spatial relation. Otherwise matter would serve no purpose in the power's existence.

Existence comes first in the order of nature. If a material power could act without position, the argument would contradict itself: acting requires existence, and this power's existence is assumed to require matter.

Parts of a measured whole resemble the whole in kind and name. If each part can be understood like the whole, and there are infinitely many parts potentially, there would be infinitely many intelligible forms. The argument uses “potentially” to expose the conflict between divisibility and intelligibility.
This division is different from the first division into spatial parts, but the spatial division follows from the assumption that the form occupies a position.

We could never fully picture a thing through infinitely many parts. Also, if broader kinds and defining features differed in nature and were arranged in different positions, the account would imply indivisible parts of matter.
“Reality” here means the whole shared nature that is understood. Its individual examples are sensed, but not as the universal nature itself.
“Its mode of existence” means its material mode of being; existence is what a thing is, in a particular way.

The passage admits two readings. First, understanding may be a relationship to the thing's real nature, considered apart from direction, place, time, and other bodily conditions. On this account the nature exists in the material world but is not grasped by the senses, because the senses encounter it mixed with features foreign to what it is. Only the intellect grasps it. As Avicenna says in the passage quoted earlier from the Beginning and Return, being mixed with other things does not destroy a thing's own nature.

Second, understanding may mean removing some features, namely those that are incidental, while keeping the essential ones and bringing them into the mind. This is not the same as the earlier account of abstraction from sensation. The first reading suits those who deny that things have existence in the mind; the second need not deny mental existence at first, though a closer examination makes the problem return.

Both readings face a serious difficulty. The natures under discussion include the ability to have dimensions among their essential features, and divisibility among what follows from them. A thing's essential features cannot simply be taken away. The same difficulty troubles anyone who says the difference between universal and particular knowledge lies only in how a single object is perceived, rather than in any difference in what is known.

The author's view offers a clearer solution. The intellectual reality exists in a new, luminous manner of being, not here in the material world stripped of a few properties. Abstraction means that this lower mode of existence is gathered into a higher one. The 'earth' of that understanding is no longer this earth, and the 'heaven' is folded away. Words such as 'substance' or 'capable of dimensions' apply to the idea in the mind as an idea, not as bodily conditions actually present there. Arguments for mental existence establish no more than this. What makes such concepts true of lower things is that the higher intellectual existence contains their reality in a more complete way.
The ascent in the argument is that this new mode of existence may not be merely another nonmaterial mode; it is specifically intellectual.

“Outside” here means the material world. This does not mean that images have no external existence in cases such as dreams, illness, or spiritual perception. A person may perceive something that exists in the soul, or at a higher level, rather than in bodily matter. Even a person of sound mind cannot always tell by sensation alone whether an image exists materially. The matter must be settled through proof or by consulting someone with knowledge of these realities.
In other words, such judgment belongs to the intellect's first principles, not to the senses.
Or through an internal imbalance, as in a fever dream.

The sensory powers are called “sensible qualities” in two respects: as representations of things, and as qualities belonging to the soul. They represent things that are sensed in themselves; in that sense they refer to the objects of perception.
As representations, these qualities have a weaker existence, mixed with nonexistence, unlike the pure existence they represent.

These forms are “human,” “horse,” and so on when considered in their own reality, not as images that represent lower things. On the view that intellects have no essences, they are even beyond being substances.
The sentence may be read as giving the reason for the divisions that follow, or as introducing a point whose conclusion is understood from the earlier discussion.
The author has already argued that sensory, imaginal, and estimative knowledge are one kind of knowing existence; there are two modes of knowing existence.
He does not separately define these kinds of existence or knowledge because he explains the corresponding kinds of knowers below.
“Animal souls” here means souls after they have left earthly bodies. Souls still joined to earthly bodies belong to the third, incomplete level.

This refers to bodies. Someone might object that, if images in knowledge exist in themselves rather than in matter, forms that stand in matter should not count as knowledge. The author includes them because they are close to the directly sensed forms that count as objects of knowledge. They depend on the positions of material objects, though only incidentally.
“Existence” here means luminous, knowing existence, not existence in every sense. This is clear from the reference to forms of knowledge.
The comparison is with mystics who include this world among the Divine Presences and as a place where the Divine appears. “Effects” means the scattered material existences.
This includes both the forms understood by us and those understood by others.

The first phrase points to the view held by Aristotle’s followers, according to which forms are imprinted in souls. The second points to the Illuminationist view, according to which these forms subsist on their own in an imaginal world.

Another possibility is that those who glide are intellects, those who race ahead are the universal souls of the heavenly spheres, and those who manage affairs are the souls within those spheres. In Illuminationist terms, the intellect is the overpowering light and the soul the governing light. Or the phrases may refer respectively to fixed realities in the realm of knowledge, the intellects, and the spheres, including both their bodies and souls.

“Mirror” here means the means by which something is revealed. If it means an instrument used to look at something else, the relation is the reverse: material and imaginal things should be mirrors for intellectual realities. Those who attend to particulars make universal and imaginal forms into mirrors of material particulars, treating them as weak even though they are strong in themselves.

The Persian verse calls even the realm of oneness something that seems not to exist: “Leave what is not but appears to be; seek what is but appears not to be.” The author's explanation is that, as beings living in nature, we do not have the kind of dependent existence that would connect us directly with that higher realm. Another reading is that this realm has no separate existence at all: its existence is wholly absorbed in God's. As the verse has it, “We were exalted letters, not yet spoken”; and another Persian line says, “When I became empty of my own existence, I knew of none but God.” As for imaginal forms, their existence is the kind of existence known to us through outward things; the word for what is in Plato's saying concerns the world of the senses.

Earlier arguments for Platonic forms show that the concepts “human,” “horse,” and the rest can be true of a separate intellectual being. They do not show that these concepts are its true essences, or that such a being is an intellectual individual of the natural kind.
